name: Giddings-Strominger Wormhole
description: A space of four dimensions and no time, Steven B. Giddings and Andrew Strominger's axion wormhole of 1988: two regions of flat space joined at a throat, a 3-sphere of radius $a$ held open by the field strength of an axion. Cut in half at the throat, it describes a closed baby universe budding off flat space.
convention: The length $a$ is the radius of the throat and the space's only parameter. All four coordinates are spatial, so no component carries a factor of $c$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to arc length. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history:
Four dimensions of space and none of time make up this geometry, $$ds^2 =  rac{dr^2}{1 - a^4/r^4} + r^2\,d\Omega_3^2,$$ where $d\Omega_3^2$ is the round metric of the unit 3-sphere and each value of $r$ labels a 3-sphere of radius $r$ [hebecker2018]. The 3-spheres shrink to a smallest one of radius $a$, the throat, and open out again beyond it, so that two regions of flat space of four dimensions meet there [giddings1988, hebecker2018]. An axion's field strength $H$, a 3-form, threads every 3-sphere with the same flux and holds the throat open [giddings1988]. The curvature scalar is $R = -6a^4/r^6$, and the Einstein tensor, which carries the field's stress, has $G^r{}_r = -3a^4/r^6$ along the radius and $3a^4/r^6$ along each direction on the sphere. Embedded in flat space of three dimensions, a slice through the throat makes a funnel whose two sheets level off at a height $\sqrt{\pi}\,\Gamma(1/4)\,a/(4\Gamma(3/4)) \approx 1.311a$ above and below it.¶Steven B. Giddings and Andrew Strominger published the solution in 1988, coupling to gravity "an axion (described by a rank-three antisymmetric tensor field strength)", in the words of their abstract [giddings1988]. They showed that an instanton changing the topology of a flat space needs a Ricci tensor with a negative eigenvalue somewhere [giddings1988]. An ordinary scalar field gives $R_{\mu
u} = 
abla_\mu\phi
abla_
u\phi$ and no negative eigenvalue. For the axion, whose Euclidean stress is the scalar's with the opposite sign, "the eigenvalues are non-positive and instantons are indeed possible" [giddings1988]. Edward Witten traced the difference to scaling in 2026: with the metric scaled by a constant, the curvature term and the 3-form's term of the action "scale oppositely" and balance at a throat of definite size; a scalar's term scales as the curvature's does, so no balance is possible [witten2026]. The axion charge $n$ carried through the throat fixes its radius, with $a^2$ in proportion to $n$, and the solution holds semiclassically while $a$ is well above the Planck length [giddings1988, witten2026].¶Giddings and Strominger cut the space in half through the throat, where the 3-sphere is a minimal surface [giddings1988]. Each half represents a tunnelling from flat space $\mathbb{R}^3$ to $\mathbb{R}^3$ together with a separate 3-sphere, which they called "the nucleation of a Planck-sized baby Robertson-Walker universe" [giddings1988]. The minimal 3-sphere has no extrinsic curvature and $H$ lies along it, so the fields continue to real time as a closed Robertson-Walker universe of radius $a$, created "at its moment of time symmetry and maximal radius" [giddings1988]. The baby universe carries off $n$ units of axion charge, and an observer left in $\mathbb{R}^3$ measures the charge change by $-n$ [giddings1988].¶George V. Lavrelashvili, V. A. Rubakov, and P. G. Tinyakov had argued in 1987 that quantum coherence may be lost when closed universes of Planck size split off flat space, and bounded the rate of such splitting from the oscillations of neutral kaons [lavrelashvili1987]. Stephen Hawking drew the same conclusion in 1988: an observer in the flat region cannot measure the state of the closed universes that branch off, so "the final state would appear to be a mixed quantum state" [hawking1988]. Giddings and Strominger estimated the effect on kaons in a gas of their instantons and found that it "can be large" unless a small parameter suppresses the instantons [giddings1988]. Sidney Coleman found within the year that the wormholes add only local interactions, with coefficients that are operators on the baby universes, so that an observer reads their eigenvalues as constants of nature and sees no loss of coherence [coleman1988, hebecker2018].¶Coleman went on to argue that "if wormholes exist, they have the effect of making the cosmological constant vanish" [coleman1988]. In his argument the wave function of the universe with the no-boundary condition of James Hartle and Hawking peaks like a delta function where the cosmological constant is zero, driven by an infrared divergence as the otherwise disconnected universe grows without bound [coleman1988]. He called the theory "doubly a house built on sand", since it rests on wormhole dynamics and on the Euclidean formulation of quantum gravity [coleman1988]. Jonathan J. Halliwell and Raymond Laflamme found a wormhole held open by a conformally coupled scalar field in 1989, its 3-spheres growing as $\sqrt{R_0^2 + 	au^2}$ with the distance $	au$ from a throat of radius $R_0$, "a much simpler analytic form" [halliwell1989]. Their wormholes differ from the axion's in that the effective gravitational constant can become negative [halliwell1989].¶Giddings and Strominger had also found that the massless dilaton of string theory "can suppress the tunneling" [giddings1988]. Arthur Hebecker, Thomas Mikhail and Pablo Soler reviewed the subject in 2018, recording that such wormholes exist in the Euclidean supergravity theories that come from string theory and that a dilute gas of them can break the axion's shift symmetry and give it a potential [hebecker2018]. The solution has the negative modes that every Euclidean saddle of gravity has through its conformal factor, and they called the meaning of any further negative modes "still an open question" [hebecker2018]. Thomas Hertog, Brecht Truijen and Thomas Van Riet found in 2019 perturbations concentrated in the neck that lower the action [hertog2019], and Gregory J. Loges, Gary Shiu and Nidhi Sudhir, holding the 3-form fixed at the boundary, found in 2022 "a perturbatively stable Euclidean saddle" [loges2022]. To Witten, writing in 2026, it is "the prototype of a Euclidean wormhole solution of Einstein gravity coupled to matter", and in the language of the scalar dual to its 2-form the throat has no semiclassical description [witten2026].

related.text: The wormhole with a time that Homer Ellis and Kirill Bronnikov found in 1973, its throat held open by a phantom scalar field [ellis1973, bronnikov1973]. Embedded in flat space, a slice through its throat climbs as $\ell\,\mathrm{arccosh}(r/\ell)$, with $\ell$ its throat radius, and never levels off.

With redshift function $\Phi = 0$ and shape function $b = a^4/r^3$, Michael Morris and Kip Thorne's wormhole has at each moment the radial profile of this space, $dr^2/(1 - a^4/r^4)$, with 2-spheres for its 3-spheres, and the same embedding diagram. Its throat needs matter whose tension exceeds its energy density [morris1988].

The closed Friedmann universe with the energy of an axion's field in it, continued to imaginary time, is this space [giddings1988]. Cut at the throat, this space continues back to that universe at radius $a$, "created at its moment of time symmetry and maximal radius" [giddings1988].

The spaces of four dimensions with no time that Stephen Hawking defined as gravitational instantons in 1977, smooth solutions of Einstein's equations without matter [hawking1977]. Giddings and Strominger drew their wormhole, which has an axion's field in it, as "a gravitational instanton with two asymptotically Euclidean regions" [giddings1988].
Albert Einstein and Nathan Rosen's bridge of 1935, two sheets of space joined at a smallest sphere, which is a horizon [einstein1935].

Another tunnelling described by a Euclidean solution round in four dimensions, a bubble of lower vacuum energy appearing in a false vacuum, which Sidney Coleman and Frank De Luccia worked out with gravity in 1980 [coleman1980]. Coleman turned to these wormholes in 1988 and argued that they make the cosmological constant vanish [coleman1988].

A gravitational instanton given a time: Euclidean Taub-NUT space with $-c^2dt^2$ added, a static vacuum of five dimensions that four dimensions see as a magnetic monopole [sorkin1983, grossperry1983].

coordinates.name: Areal Radius
domains: r = a \;\text{(the throat, where the two halves meet)}

parameters.description: Radius of the throat, the smallest 3-sphere, a length

coordinates.convention: We use the areal radius $r$, a length, and angles $(\chi, \theta, \phi)$ on the 3-sphere of radius $r$. The chart covers one half of the wormhole, and the other half is its copy glued on at $r = a$.

coordinates.name: Proper Distance (Giddings-Strominger)

parameters.description: Radius of the throat, the smallest 3-sphere, a length
Areal radius, a length, the radius of the 3-sphere at the proper distance $\rho$ from the throat; on the wormhole it solves $(\partial_\rho r)^2 = 1 - a^4/r^4$ with $r(0) = a$

coordinates.convention: We use the proper distance $\rho$ from the throat, a length, negative on the far half, and angles $(\chi, \theta, \phi)$ on the 3-sphere of radius $r$. The radius $r$ is a free function of $\rho$, and no component assumes the equation $(\partial_\rho r)^2 = 1 - a^4/r^4$, whose solution with $r(0) = a$ is the wormhole.
geodesics: \ddot{\rho} - r\,\partial_\rho r\,\dot{\chi}^2 - r\,\partial_\rho r\,\sin^2\chi\,\dot{\theta}^2 - r\,\partial_\rho r\,\sin^2\chi\sin^2\theta\,\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: Conformal (Loges-Shiu-Sudhir)

parameters.description: Radius of the throat, the smallest 3-sphere, a length

coordinates.convention: We use the pure number $\eta$, negative on the far half, and angles $(\chi, \theta, \phi)$ on the 3-sphere of radius $r$, with $r^2 = a^2\cosh(2\eta)$.
